To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the exchange rate is not a relevant criterion in the selection of the candidate countries, and that the exchange rate should not play a major role in the strategy of the CEECs towards the EU.
the extra trade induced by fixing the currency, as in the case of the Euro, is close to nil.

(i) there is no evidence that fixing the exchange rate regime fosters trade; (ii) the benefit from membership of the EMU cannot be explained by transaction costs; (iii) the external constraint is affected by monetary and fiscal policies; (iv) the co-variation between East-West business cycles can be explained by intra-industry trade; and (v) the choice of the exchange rate regime should not be the key criterion for entering the EU.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following question: is it possible to find an appropriate exchange rate regime in transition countries?
the following question: What is the appropriate exchange rate arrangement for countries aiming at entering the EMU?.

the question of whether the adoption of a single currency by a group of countries, such as the EU, is a sufficient condition for trade integration, and if so, what the optimal exchange rate regime is for countries aiming at entering this currency union.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

there is no clear-cut evidence that the exchange rate is a good indicator of the degree of convergence of a country towards EU standards, and therefore, no clear-cut evidence of an optimal exchange rate regime.
there is no evidence in support of a fixed exchange regime, but no evidence against it, either.
the exchange rate is irrelevant, as long as the EU is willing to accept any candidate country.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there is no evidence in favour of fixing the exchange rate in CEECs.
the exchange rate is not a good instrument for macro-economic policy, but a good instrument for trade policy.
the EU is a club of countries with a common currency, but not necessarily with a common exchange rate regime, as the EU is not a CU.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the exchange rate should not be a major criterion for the EU accession, as it is not a major determinant of the economic performance of Transition Countries.
the EU should not be seen as a monetary union, but rather as a trade union.
the choice of the exchange rate regime should be left to the country’s own choice, and should not be imposed by the EU.
